ansatz: brute-force over the complete x-range n/4<x<=3n/4, sufficient e|(nx) divisibility test with a 1/w->1/(w+1)+1/(w(w+1)) split for a 3rd term
why_failed: never fires for n = 1 (mod 4) (empirically confirmed on all n<5000); the fully general divisor-pair completion for that residue class is only ~O(n) per n in the worst case, capping the fully-verified frontier at N=10000 (52s for the n=1 mod4 residue alone), 13 orders of magnitude short of the published N=10^17 sieve which relies on covering congruences we did not implement

ansatz: incremental exact factorial (running product) + gmpy2.isqrt exact perfect-square check per n
why_failed: big-integer multiplication cost grows faster than linearly as n! gains digits, so wall time scales superlinearly (8.44s to n=20000, 103.44s to n=60000); this naive approach cannot approach the published N=10^9 frontier, which almost certainly filters n via modular quadratic-residue sieving before ever forming n! for a survivor -- the wrong bottleneck to be fighting with more brute force

ansatz: numpy divisor-count sieve (tau[d::d]+=1 for d=1..N) with running max of m+tau(m), pure per-d Python outer loop
why_failed: outer loop over d is O(N) unvectorized Python regardless of the vectorized inner slice op, capping N at ~10^7 in the time available (10^8 timed out at 120s) -- a C-level or fully-vectorized (e.g. sieve-of-multiples via cumulative bincount) sieve is needed to close more of the gap to the kernel-checked N=10^9 published frontier

ansatz: sparse enumeration of powerful (2-full) numbers via n=a^2*b^3 up to N, scan sorted set for three consecutive integers
why_failed: not a search-depth failure (method reaches N=10^13 in ~34s and could go higher) but a calibration failure: no published numeric search bound exists to compare against -- the literature's strongest statements are structural (Beckon's mod-36 residue narrowing) or abc-conditional, not computational, so 'push N further' has no natural target and adds little

ansatz: sparse enumeration of powerful (2-full) and cube-full (3-full) numbers via a^2*b^3 / a^3*b^4*c^5, scan powerful set for n with n+1 in the cube-full set

ansatz: sparse enumeration of cube-full (3-full) numbers via n=a^3*b^4*c^5 up to N, scan sorted set for two consecutive integers
why_failed: not a search-depth failure (method reaches N=10^18 in ~11s) but the same calibration failure as erdos-0364-a: no known example or published search bound exists for genuinely-3-full consecutive pairs (the small pairs the literature cites for related questions were confirmed by direct factorization to be only 2-full, not 3-full, on one side) -- nothing to ratio our frontier against
